title: Designing cancer drugs
summary: The drug-discovery pipeline, chemical space, binding free energy and why a kilocalorie matters, structure prediction, generative AI — and the KRAS story end to end.

shots.title:
Designing
cancer drugs.
shots.subtitle: Where computation already earns its keep.
shots.narration: Drug discovery is the oncology problem most often named as a quantum application. To judge that, you need to know the pipeline and where classical computation already works.

Pick a target, find hits that bind it, optimise them into a lead with the right potency and safety, nominate a candidate, and go to trials. Computation helps most in finding hits and optimising leads.

shots.text: Chemical space is vast: estimates of drug-like molecules run from **10²³** to **10⁶⁰**.
shots.narration: The search space is vast and poorly known: estimates of the number of drug-like molecules range from ten to the twenty-three to ten to the sixty. One enumeration lists a hundred and sixty-six billion small molecules of up to seventeen atoms.

notes: lead optimisation needs about fivefold accuracy
shots.narration: Binding strength is free energy. Delta G equals R T log K d, so at room temperature every one point three six kilocalories per mole means tenfold tighter binding. Optimising leads needs predictions good to about fivefold.

shots.text: A kilocalorie per mole is also **chemical accuracy** — the target of quantum chemistry. Same scale, same problem.
shots.narration: Notice the scale: about one kilocalorie per mole is also what quantum chemists call chemical accuracy. That is not a coincidence; it is the scale at which binding predictions become useful.

shots.text: Free-energy perturbation (FEP+) was validated on **200** ligands and in prospective projects — classical physics plus sampling.
shots.narration: Classical physics-based methods already reach that regime for many systems: one free-energy perturbation protocol was validated on two hundred ligands across targets and in live drug projects.

shots.text: **AlphaFold** (2021) predicts protein structures near experimental accuracy; **AlphaFold 3** (2024) adds ligands, DNA and RNA.
shots.narration: Structure prediction changed the field. AlphaFold, in 2021, predicted protein structures competitive with experiment in most test cases. AlphaFold 3 extended this to complexes with drugs, DNA and RNA — and the work won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

shots.text: Classical generative AI designed **DDR1** kinase inhibitors in **21 days** — the baseline any quantum generative model must beat.
shots.narration: And generative AI already designs molecules: a classical model proposed DDR1 kinase inhibitors in twenty-one days, with two active in cells. Keep that baseline in mind for the quantum case study later.

events.label: AMG 510
events.detail: first G12C inhibitor in the clinic

shots.narration: The KRAS story ties it together. The most frequently mutated oncogene was undruggable for decades. A pocket was found in 2013, the first clinical inhibitor reported in 2019, and sotorasib approved in 2021.

shots.text: Where might quantum fit? Where classical **electronic structure** struggles: covalent bonds forming and breaking, metals, excited states.
shots.narration: So where might quantum computers fit? Where classical electronic-structure methods struggle: covalent bonds forming and breaking, as in sotorasib; metal centres, as in the enzymes that metabolise drugs; and excited states. That is the next unit.

steps.title: How much free energy is a better drug?
steps.brief: Use ΔG = RT ln K_d. Guess first, then check.

props.question: A lead binds its target with K_d = 1 μM. You need 10 nM. How much more binding free energy (kcal/mol, at 25 °C) must the new molecule find?
props.reveal: 1 μM → 10 nM is a hundredfold, two factors of ten: 2 × 1.36 ≈ 2.7 kcal/mol Small energies, large consequences: the whole optimisation lives within a few kcal/mol.

questions.prompt: A modification improves ΔG by 4.09 kcal/mol at 25 °C. By what factor does binding tighten?
A method's binding free energies have an error of 1.36 kcal/mol. Roughly what factor of uncertainty is that in K_d?
questions.explain: One factor of ten — twice the roughly fivefold accuracy lead optimisation needs.

questions.prompt: What did AlphaFold 3 add over AlphaFold?
options: Faster folding of single proteins only
Joint structures of complexes including small molecules, nucleic acids and ions
Binding free energies to chemical accuracy
questions.explain: AlphaFold 3 predicts complexes, with much better protein–ligand accuracy than docking tools — but it predicts structure, not binding free energy.

steps.title: Homework 10 · A drug, molecule by molecule

fields.label: 1. Find a crystal structure of KRAS G12C bound to sotorasib or a related inhibitor in the Protein Data Bank (rcsb.org). Record the PDB ID and describe, in words, how the drug binds.
2. If your method's error is ±1 kcal/mol, what fold-range of K_d does that imply? Is that good enough to rank ten close analogues? Show the arithmetic.
3. List the steps in the pipeline where computation is used, and mark which you think are limited by electronic-structure accuracy (a quantum opportunity) and which by data, sampling or biology.
